title: The stash will not pop: conflicts, and the branch that fixes them
summary: You stashed, then the branch moved underneath you. Popping now conflicts. Resolve it, and learn about `git stash branch`, which sidesteps the problem entirely.
mental_model: A stash remembers the commit it was made on. Applying it elsewhere is a three-way merge between that base, your stashed work, and wherever you are now — so it conflicts exactly like any merge.

steps.title: Stash work, then let the branch move
steps.why: You park a pool-size experiment. While it is parked, a colleague's change lands on the same line. The stash still remembers the old base — that mismatch is the conflict waiting to happen.

actions.run: git commit -q -a -m "Tune pool and timeout after the incident"

steps.expect: One stash, and a new commit touching the same line.

steps.title: Look at the stash before applying it
steps.why: `stash show -p` prints the diff without touching anything. Reading this first tells you whether the parked work is still worth restoring — often, days later, it is not.
steps.expect: The pool-size change from 5 to 25, against the old base.

steps.title: Pop, and hit the conflict
steps.why: Three versions of the same line: base 5, stash 25, current 10. Git cannot choose, so you get markers — the same experience as any merge conflict, because it is one.

steps.title: Notice the stash was NOT dropped
steps.why: On a clean pop the entry is deleted. On a conflicted one git keeps it, deliberately — so a botched resolution cannot cost you the work. This is the safest failure mode in git.

verify.label: the stash survived the failed pop

steps.title: Resolve and clean up by hand
steps.why: Take 25 from the experiment and the new timeout from the commit. Then drop the stash yourself — since pop did not, you must, or it lingers forever.

verify.label: the stash entry was dropped manually

steps.title: The better route: stash branch
steps.why: `git stash branch <name>` creates a branch at the stash's ORIGINAL base commit, applies the stash there, and drops it. Same base as when you stashed, so it cannot conflict — then you merge or rebase deliberately.

actions.run: git commit -q -a -m "Adopt the larger pool size"

steps.expect: A new branch at the stash's base, work applied cleanly, no conflict, stash gone.

verify.label: you are on the new branch created from the stash
the stashed work applied without conflict
stash branch dropped the entry for you

steps.title: Integrate deliberately
steps.why: Now the experiment is a branch like any other. Commit it and merge when you are ready — you have converted an awkward stash restore into an ordinary merge, which is a much better problem to have.

verify.label: the second experiment became a real branch
no stash entries were left behind
verify.hint: a conflicted pop keeps the entry — drop it yourself once resolved

verify.label: main kept the resolved pool size and the newer timeout

pitfalls: A conflicted `pop` leaves the entry in the list. Forget to drop it and you will re-apply the same work weeks later, wondering where it came from.
`git stash branch` only works cleanly if the stash's base commit still exists — after a rebase or a force push it may not.
`git stash apply` on a different branch is a three-way merge, not a copy. It can conflict even when the files look unrelated.
`git checkout -- .` while a pop is conflicted destroys the resolution in progress. Use `git checkout --merge` or drop and re-apply.
cheatsheet: read a stash before applying it
apply and drop — keeps the entry if it conflicts
new branch at the stash's base, applied cleanly
